evidence_quotes.quote: In order to compile and characterize the existing evidence on environmental health in protracted displacement, we conducted a systematic scoping review to answer the following research questions:
The most frequently discussed environmental health topic is water, with findings reported in 149 studies (70%), followed by sanitation (n=107, 50%), and then crowding (n=79, 37%) (Table 7).
Eighteen publications present findings on average water consumption per day, which ranged from one to 40 liters per capita per day (Table 8).

Of the 107 publications (50%) that report on sanitation conditions, 42 (20%) report coverage data, though measurement methods varied: 21 studies (10%) report household or population sanitation coverage, 15 (7%) measure average number of persons per latrine or toilet per person
Outcomes of environmental health conditions are reported in 136 studies (64%) and were categorized as health (n=133, 62%) or livelihood (n=10, 5%).

National laws and policies are frequently described as obstacles; specifically, policies which require refugees to stay in camps prevent them from seeking government health services (Mohamed et al., 2014), and laws that prevent the expansion or development of permanent camp infrastructure limit potential improvements in environmental health conditions (Hydroconseil, 2017; Rueff & Viaro, 2010).

criterion_notes.c1: Satisfied. Among 213 protracted-displacement studies mapped, 149 (70%) report on water supply conditions (sources, distribution, reliability, daily quantity, tariffs/affordability) and 107 (50%) report on sanitation conditions (latrine/sewer coverage, persons per latrine, open defecation).
criterion_notes.c2: Not satisfied under the 2026-10-13 clarification. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the review touches tangentially on institutional, legal, and governance factors because Section 3.3 catalogs 'institutional' obstacles (legal/policy environment, management challenges, NGO/sector coordination) among 43 studies reporting obstacles across all environmental health topics, briefly citing laws restricting camp expansion or permanent infrastructure (Rueff & Viaro, 2010; Hydroconseil, 2017) and camp-confinement rules affecting healthcare seeking (Mohamed et al., 2014), and Section 4.2 offers normative human-rights and SDG monitoring policy recommendations. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, however, the review fails Criterion 2: it is a broad environmental health scoping review whose exposure focus is protracted forced displacement and environmental hazards/conditions across 10 domains, not a systematic synthesis of a rule-type legal, administrative, tariff, tenure, eligibility, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access. Mentions of camp infrastructure laws and unreferenced passing mention of water tariffs/connection fees function only as brief, unanalysed macro-governance/obstacle background rather than an examined exposure-to-access mechanism.
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfied. PRISMA-guided systematic scoping review synthesizing 213 empirical peer-reviewed (n=198) and grey-literature (n=15) publications published between 1946 and 2017.
criterion_notes.c4: Satisfied descriptively. Although Section 3.2.3 defines 'outcomes' as health (diarrhea, respiratory illness, malaria; 62%) and livelihood (5%) outcomes, Section 3.2.1 descriptively reports water consumption quantity (1 to 40 liters/capita/day across 18 studies), supply interruptions, affordability concerns, and household/population sanitation and sewer coverage (42 studies).
criterion_notes.c5: Satisfied for the scoping review's own environmental-health scope (identifiable PRISMA scoping review design, protracted forcibly displaced populations, environmental conditions/contaminant exposures, and health/livelihood outcomes plus descriptive WaSH conditions), though units of analysis vary across the 213 mapped studies (camp, settlement, household, individual, school, health facility, restaurant) and no rule-type legal/administrative exposure is systematically linked to water or sanitation access outcomes.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfied. Full text is in English.

study_design: Systematic scoping review (PRISMA-guided review of 213 peer-reviewed and grey literature publications)
country: Multi-country (54 countries across Northern Africa and Western Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Central and Southern Asia, Eastern and Southeastern Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Europe and Northern America; most represented: Kenya, Sudan, Thailand)
population_and_sample: Forcibly displaced populations (refugees in 73% of studies, internally displaced persons in 27%, plus asylum seekers and climate/displaced migrants) living in protracted displacement (>2 years) across 213 publications (198 peer-reviewed, 15 grey literature), primarily in camps (86%) and settlements (9%) as well as urban/other settings (18%); mixed units of analysis across included studies (camp, settlement, household, individual, school, health facility, restaurant)
exposure: Protracted forced displacement settings (>2 years) and general environmental health conditions and microbial/chemical hazards across 10 topics (water, sanitation, crowding, vector control, energy, waste management, hand hygiene, food safety, menstrual hygiene, air quality); legal/policy factors appear only as brief descriptive obstacle categories rather than an analysed rule-type mechanism governing WaSH access
outcome: Primary review outcomes are infectious/non-communicable health outcomes (62% of studies, e.g., diarrhea, respiratory illness, malaria) and agricultural/livelihood outcomes (5%); descriptively maps water supply conditions (including per-capita water consumption in 18 studies, water sources, reliability, tariffs/affordability) and sanitation coverage (42 studies)
rationale: Exclude under E03 (Wrong exposure). Behnke et al. (2020) is a broad PRISMA scoping review mapping general environmental health conditions (water, sanitation, crowding, vector control, energy, waste, hygiene, food safety, air quality), microbial/chemical contaminants, and health/livelihood outcomes in protracted displacement (>2 years) across 213 studies. While it descriptively summarizes water quantity and sanitation coverage (c1, c3, c4) and notes 'institutional' obstacles in a general obstacle taxonomy (including two brief single-sentence citations to national laws limiting permanent camp infrastructure, alongside NGO coordination, project turnover, resource scarcity, and normative human-rights/SDG policy commentary), it does not examine or synthesize any rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, tenure, or tariff mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope clarification.
